cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: real coefficient 3 and imaginary coefficient 4, default suffix
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as the text 3+4i. Follows directly from the documented conversion "real and imaginary coefficients into a complex number of the form x + yi", with the documented default suffix "i"; the result is a text string, not a number, so there is nothing to round

cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example with the alternate engineering suffix j
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as the text 3+4j. The documentation states all complex-number functions accept "i" and "j" for suffix

cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: a pure imaginary unit, where the zero real part is suppressed
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as the text i (not 0+1i): a zero real coefficient and a unit imaginary coefficient are both elided in the canonical form. This case pins the elision rule, which is pure formatting behaviour and not derivable from arithmetic

cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: a zero imaginary part, where the imaginary term is suppressed entirely
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as the text 1 (not 1+0i). The mirror image of the previous case: a zero imaginary coefficient drops the whole imaginary term, leaving a bare real coefficient as text
Excel documents: "All complex number functions accept \"i\" and \"j\" for suffix, but neither \"I\" nor \"J\". Using uppercase results in the #VALUE! error value."
Excel documents: "If real_num is nonnumeric, COMPLEX returns the #VALUE! error value."
